speaker: Vincent Clerc
title: The Potential of Data in Global Trade | Vincent Clerc
question: In maritime shipping, why is the global energy transition a fundamentally different kind of disruption than past industry cycles?
guest: An even bigger transition in shipping is the whole energy transition and decarbonization. It's a totally different ballgame—it's like going from sail to steam, from steam to oil. Forty percent of the volume of cargo today is actually energy: forty percent of the tons moved by ships are oil, gas, and coal, and this will be replaced by something else. In the meantime, you have to use totally different propulsion energies which do not yet exist at scale, though I think they will exist. Technological progress will never be as slow as today, so we will have even more progress. We cannot rely on past extrapolation—we have to account for these exponential advances of technology. And when it comes to really decarbonizing shipping, there are data and insights possible today that were not possible five years ago.

points.core: Roughly forty percent of seaborne cargo tonnage consists of fossil fuels.
points.note: Accept: ~35-45% (around 40%) of maritime cargo weight/tons is energy commodities (oil, gas, coal) that will decline or be replaced. Do not credit: vague statements that shipping carries "a lot of oil" without the structural cargo-base magnitude.

points.core: Shipping fleets must simultaneously switch to completely new propulsion fuel technologies.
points.note: Accept: vessels themselves must transition off bunker oil to alternative/zero-carbon fuels (comparable to sail-to-steam or steam-to-oil). Do not credit: generic references to "going green" without distinguishing vessel propulsion from cargo.

points.core: Extrapolating from past historical trends fails under exponential technological change.
points.note: Accept: linear historical forecasting breaks down because fuel and maritime technologies advance non-linearly/exponentially. Do not credit: generic claims that "the future is uncertain."

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Past shipping cycles were swings in supply and demand: freight rates rose, owners over-ordered ships, capacity overshot, rates collapsed, and the market eventually rebalanced. The underlying business stayed the same, with the same cargoes, the same fuel and the same ship designs. The energy transition is structural rather than cyclical, and it hits the industry from two sides at once.

First, it changes what ships carry. Roughly a third or more of seaborne trade by tonnage is coal, crude oil, oil products and gas. As the world decarbonises, that demand declines permanently rather than rebounding, while new trades emerge in ammonia, hydrogen carriers, CO2, biofuels, critical minerals and offshore wind components.

Second, it changes how ships are powered. Regulation such as the IMO's greenhouse gas targets and the EU's emissions trading system and FuelEU Maritime rules is forcing a shift away from fuel oil, but the winning fuel (methanol, ammonia, LNG or others) remains uncertain.

Because ships last 20–25 years, owners must make large investments now under deep technological and regulatory uncertainty, with real stranded-asset risk. Waiting for the cycle to turn won't resolve it.

points.why: The candidate gives an open-ended lower estimate of roughly one-third, which does not establish a share around 40%.
The candidate commits to a shift away from fuel oil for vessel propulsion and leaves the choice of replacement fuel open.
quotes: Second, it changes how ships are powered.
is forcing a shift away from fuel oil, but the winning fuel (methanol, ammonia, LNG or others) remains uncertain.

points.why: The candidate describes technological uncertainty and stranded-asset risk without explaining why nonlinear technological progress undermines historical extrapolation.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Past maritime cycles were self-correcting swings in fleet capacity and freight demand, while historic technological shifts—sail to steam, coal to oil, and containerization—succeeded because new systems delivered greater speed, higher energy density, or lower unit costs. The global energy transition inverts those economics. Driven by regulation and carbon pricing rather than standalone commercial advantage, decarbonization requires fuels like green methanol or ammonia that are structurally costlier and less energy-dense than fuel oil, penalizing cargo space or range.

Instead of converging on one clear standard, shipowners face a fragmented multi-fuel future dependent on renewable power and port infrastructure largely outside maritime control, creating acute stranded-asset risk across twenty-five-year vessel lifespans. Most fundamentally, this disruption reshapes both how ships operate and what they carry: fossil fuels represent over a third of global seaborne trade volume, forcing shipping to overhaul its propulsion and financing just as its largest historical cargo base enters structural decline.

noweb.answer:
Past maritime cycles were reversible swings in freight supply and trade demand, and previous propulsion shifts—from sail to coal, and coal to oil—succeeded because each new fuel was cheaper, faster, and more energy-dense. Today’s energy transition inverts those economics. Zero-carbon candidates like green methanol and ammonia are structurally costlier and less energy-dense than conventional fuel oil, sacrificing cargo space and range rather than improving vessel performance. 

Because this shift is driven by regulation and carbon pricing rather than inherent commercial superiority, no single winning technology has emerged. Shipowners ordering vessels with twenty-five-year lifespans must gamble on fragmented fuel pathways locked in a chicken-and-egg standoff with external power grids, fuel producers, and port bunkering infrastructure—turning familiar cyclical timing risk into long-term stranded-asset risk. Crucially, decarbonization also transforms what ships carry, not just how they are powered: with oil, coal, and gas accounting for over a third of global seaborne trade volume, the industry must re-engineer its entire fleet at the exact moment its largest cargo markets face structural decline and rewiring.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Past shipping disruptions were mostly **cyclical**. Demand booms led to ordering sprees, overcapacity and freight-rate crashes, then scrapping and recovery. Owners could ride out a downturn because the underlying system stayed the same: the same cargoes, the same fuels and the same ship designs.

The energy transition is **structural and permanent**, and it hits the industry from two directions at once. First, it changes what ships carry. Fossil fuels (oil, coal and gas) make up roughly 40% of seaborne trade, so decarbonization will shrink or reroute those flows while new trades in critical minerals, biofuels and possibly ammonia or hydrogen grow. Second, it changes how ships are powered. Regulation such as the EU ETS, FuelEU Maritime and the IMO's emerging net-zero framework is pushing fleets away from heavy fuel oil, but there is still no clear successor fuel among LNG, methanol, ammonia and others.

Ships last 25 to 30 years, so vessels ordered today must stay compliant and competitive into the 2050s, under uncertain technology, fuel supply and regulation. That creates a real risk of stranded assets. There is no "normal" for the market to return to, so waiting out the cycle doesn't work. Owners have to make irreversible bets on a future system that hasn't settled yet.

points.why: In context, the 40% figure refers to the physical cargo mix and establishes the scale of fossil fuel flows exposed to decarbonization.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Past maritime shipping cycles were temporary imbalances between vessel supply and trade demand, driven by economic swings or overbuilding that eventually self-corrected through scrapping and freight-rate adjustments. The global energy transition, by contrast, is a permanent, regulatory-driven structural transformation that simultaneously disrupts both how ships operate and what they carry.

Operationally, decarbonization mandates like the IMO's net-zero framework and regional carbon pricing require replacing fossil bunker fuels with green alternatives such as ammonia, methanol, or hydrogen. Because vessels last 20 to 25 years and no single fuel or global bunkering network has emerged as the clear winner, shipowners face severe technological uncertainty and stranded-asset risk, requiring coordinated investment across shipyards, energy producers, and ports.

Simultaneously, the transition reshapes maritime demand itself. Fossil fuels—coal, crude oil, and gas—have historically accounted for roughly a third of seaborne trade by volume; as those flows decline, shipping must reorient its fleets and routes around emerging clean-energy supply chains.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Past shipping downturns have typically come from a mismatch between cargo demand and fleet capacity. Freight rates fall, owners scrap older ships or order fewer new ones, and the market eventually rebalances. The global energy transition changes what that market looks like. It reshapes what ships carry and where they carry it as demand for fossil fuels shifts and new energy supply chains emerge. It also changes how ships are powered as emissions rules tighten.

Those changes create a different investment problem. A ship ordered today may trade for decades, yet its future fuel costs, access to bunkering, and resale value depend on decisions by regulators, ports, fuel producers, and cargo owners. A recovery in freight rates can restore earnings, but it cannot make an incompatible vessel economical to run or bring back a cargo trade that has disappeared.

points.why: The response describes shifting fossil fuel demand but gives no estimate of fossil fuels’ share of seaborne cargo tonnage.
The response identifies a change in how ships are powered but does not establish that fleets must switch from conventional bunker fuel to new propulsion fuels.
The response describes investment uncertainty but does not explain how accelerating technological change undermines forecasts based on historical trends.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Past shipping cycles mainly changed how many ships the market needed. Demand rose or fell, freight rates moved, and owners adjusted by ordering ships or scrapping them. The energy transition also changes what kinds of ships will be viable and what cargoes they will carry.

A vessel ordered today may operate for decades. Its owner must choose a propulsion system before knowing which low-emission fuels will be affordable, which ports will supply them, or how much future emissions rules will cost. At the same time, declining coal or oil trade can erode demand for some ships while new cargoes create demand for others. A freight-rate recovery can absorb excess capacity, but it cannot by itself supply a missing fuel network or restore a disappearing trade.
